🔸The Loss of a Mediator🔸

If we were to describe any figure with a single word, the word that fits Ayatollah Seyyed Mousa Shubeyri Zanjani (who passed away last night) is "mediator."

Though he was considered among the traditionalist jurists of the seminary in his jurisprudential leanings, and though—as is clear from his scattered remarks and writings (including in the highly readable book collection "A Sip from the Sea")—he was not without taste or conviction in politics and history, he nonetheless had his own distinct and particular social and political bearing. Over the past two or three decades, he played a role that others were incapable of playing: that of "mediator" between the system and the religious currents and individuals it had cast out. Shubeyri Zanjani was a "dragoman" for translating between two groups that did not understand each other's language. For this reason, knots that could not be untied through law and conventional political methods were sometimes loosened by a single phone call from him, and challenges that could have spiraled into crises were sometimes defused by a single piece of advice from him. These mediations were, of course, typically behind the scenes and kept out of the media—and that, too, was part of his way.

Because of this role he played, Shubeyri was beloved by all sides. He kept company with the martyred Leader and also performed funeral prayers for clerics critical of the system, and the door of his home remained open every day to all political and religious currents. Undoubtedly, his humble and tolerant character also played a part in this.

In religious matters as well, although he is classified among the traditional jurists, he took a different approach there too. Unlike them, he did not use his position, standing, and influence to pursue religious identity-driven concerns, nor did he seek to pile up a calendar of Shiite commemorations and to fatten rituals. On the contrary, he was critical of the excessive expansion of rituals.

That said, if the loss of Mr. Shubeyri Zanjani is a scholarly loss for the seminaries, it will be a functional and institutional blow to the system and to Iranian society as well—one that could disrupt the system's relations with certain seminary and religious currents. Though Shubeyri was not counted among the first-tier maraji in terms of the organizational hierarchy of the marja'iyya, had no vast apparatus or numerous offices, and his following did not extend beyond a circle of certain seminary insiders and his fellow townspeople, his loss creates a void in the institution of Shiite marja'iyya in Iran that cannot be filled—especially in the current critical conditions, when Iranian society needs more than ever those who can play the role of mediator in various arenas.

The B&R Program – Part Three

My take is that you can learn as much about China's ideas, strategies, and orientations from B&R as you can from BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.

I know that comparing a program to an organization, a forum, or a treaty is flawed. But I'm making this point in the sense that within B&R, China's hands are free and it isn't bogged down in coordinating with multiple governments. At the same time, it has to allocate resources directly to projects. So maybe in BRICS and the SCO, there are moments of pleasantries and what you might call political flirting, but in B&R there's no room for those games. They have to genuinely lay out their decisions and policies clearly and transparently, and actually implement them.

Although it has never been officially stated outright, in my view (a personal interpretation), one of the main reasons China at one point encouraged Iran and Saudi Arabia to negotiate and clear up their grievances probably comes back to B&R. Setting aside the things that get written on paper, signed, and photographed (Iranian officials have racked up plenty of those photos with China), in practice China's largest volume of B&R cooperation in our region has been with Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Iraq. Cooperation with Iran hasn't been insignificant either. But sanctions, banking restrictions, and other considerations have made the scale of cooperation different.

The horizon China has for B&R spans several decades. And naturally, it aligns the decisions, policies, and resources it allocates with this project as much as possible.

In a way, you could call it a super-framework for economic and investment affairs.

By the way, Pakistan is also one of China's close partners in this program. Of course, beyond all that, Pakistan has a very deep relationship with China. In the media, it's usually referred to as an ironclad relationship (China doesn't throw around such terms and expressions lightly).

The last point worth paying attention to is that China insists strongly on defining its interactions — whether in B&R or in other cooperations — as a partnership, and emphasizes that it is not the type for alliance. The logic is that a partnership makes sense between two parties. But an alliance is usually formed against a third country, or assumes (or creates) a third rival.

This strategy leads China, in many instances, not to behave the way its partners expect it to.

The late Seyyed Mahmoud Taleghani, in the seven months of his life after the 1979 Revolution, enjoyed a popularity beyond imagination. The resonance of his clear voice in the environment of the University of Tehran acted like the blowing of a pleasant and gentle breeze upon hearts fearful and anxious about the fire of the power-seeking conflicts of the age. His voice was full of a spiritual freshness yet accompanied by much sorrow, warning, and deep concern about the future. It was as if he knew what lay ahead. He knew well many of his peers and the various political organizations of that day, and he knew precisely what goal each of them was pursuing behind their pompous and hollow slogans. He did not enter into the game of any of them, nor did he consent to the elimination and exclusion of any of them. He tried to offer a rule for the coexistence of all of them within a pluralist framework, but it was as if he knew how the story would unfold! He concealed his suffering, sorrow, distress, dissatisfaction, and desperation, but it seemed that the poisonous draught of self-consumption and self-restraint wore down his frail and ailing body and took his life. If you tell a client you can do something (at no extra cost) two weeks earlier than the norm, and you see they don't appreciate it and easily pass it by, take a look at your calendar and say, 'I made a mistake.' In that scene, when the wind sweeps through the meadow, it seems as if a glimpse of paradise appears on earth. The man's voice resonated in my ears like the recitation of a poem, as delicate as the murmur of a gentle autumn rain. I said to myself, how could such a seemingly rough alphabet produce words so fluent, delicate, and sweet? Moscow's air temperature was a few degrees higher than St. Petersburg's, but fortunately, it remained at a mild and pleasant level. There is no room left for denial! The Khorasan newspaper, which usually supports the positions of Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the Speaker of the Parliament, in response to Masoud Pezeshkian's explicit references to the problems afflicting society and the country, wrote: "A large part of society, upon hearing these problems—especially from someone responsible for solving them—will surely feel bad about the future. This is exactly the outcome the enemy pursues in its media."

In reality, the story is exactly the opposite! When the president honestly and sincerely raises the problems of society, not only does a large part of society not feel bad, but they actually feel a bit of relief knowing that senior officials are aware of the multitude of problems in their lives and are informed of the dimensions of the issues!

The multitude of problems are too evident and tangible for the people to be ignored or concealed. Therefore, when an official tries to ignore or downplay the issues, society concludes that these people are trapped and imprisoned in their own closed bubble, unaware of what is happening at the societal level, and thus they are out of touch with reality!

For this reason, people feel extremely bad and bitter, thinking to themselves: When these people don't even know what situation we are in and how much we suffer from all these calamities, how can we expect them to solve any problem?

In contrast, when someone in the position of president acknowledges the problems, people say to themselves, at least thank goodness they themselves know what is going on!

The truth is that the era of sweeping garbage under the rug is over. You can sweep a single piece of garbage under the rug to hide it from guests, but a large number of them cannot be hidden. Just as the stench of accumulated trash seeps out from under the rug and exposes the homeowner's concealment, so too does the volume of society's big and small problems.

Those who, for whatever purpose, deny the volume of society's problems or downplay them do not create hope in people but rather fuel their anger and dissatisfaction.

When someone denies an object right before our eyes, the only feeling we get is that they are taking us for a fool! Human beings become provoked and angered when they are assumed to be fools.
